title: Traffic shaping and priority fanout standards
author: Aisha Patel
body:
Overview
======

This document defines standards for traffic shaping, request priority fanout, and related operational controls across Redwood’s inference platform. It covers API-level shaping, per-tenant and global priority classes, model fanout rules, backpressure and circuit-breaker behavior, observability and SLOs, plus rollout and testing guidance. The goal is predictable performance and graceful degradation during contention while preserving fairness and cost predictability.

Scope
-----
- Applies to all user-facing inference endpoints (generation, chat, embeddings, rerank) served by Hosted, Dedicated, and Private runtimes.
- Includes per-tenant shaping, global ingress throttles, model-variant fanout, and priority routing used by internal control-plane and per-customer routing policies.
- Excludes low-level GPU kernel scheduling (covered in runtime docs) and network-level QoS applied by cloud provider (see infra network topo).

Motivation & Background
-----------------------
Redwood supports mixed workloads: latency-sensitive interactive traffic and large batch/async requests. Without disciplined shaping and priority-aware fanout, hotspots can:
- Increase tail latency for premium customers
- Cause excessive cache/kv churn across hosts
- Escalate cost by triggering unnecessary model fallbacks or overprovisioned capacity

We adopt a layered approach: lightweight API ingress shaping, tenant-aware scheduling, controlled model-level fanout, and circuit-breakers at the model/instance boundary. This document records the standards and concrete configuration suggested for new services and updates to existing services.

Standards (high level)
----------------------
1) Priority classes
   - class=interactive (highest): short requests, p95 latency SLOs, enterprise customers; preemptible only per policy.
   - class=background: batch jobs and async generation; higher throughput tolerance, lower priority.
   - class=best_effort: free-tier, burst-limited.

2) Ingress shaping (per-route)
   - Rate limit tokens: default 300 req/s per route for interactive; configurable via product plan.
   - Burst window: allow bursts up to 3x sustained for interactive, 1.2x for background.
   - Leaky-bucket queueing with max-queue-depth 200 (interactive) and 1000 (background). Excess is rejected with HTTP 429 and x-retry-after header.

3) Fanout rules (model selection and routing)
   - Primary fanout: when a request requires model-side parallelism (e.g., multi-encoder or split-LLM pipelines), fanout must be limited to at most 4 replicas by default and documented in the model manifest.
   - Overflow fanout: On queue pressure, automatically reduce fanout to 1 and prefer lower-cost quantized variants (see model manifest tags: fallback_candidates).
   - Deterministic ordering: fanout router must try replicas in affinity order to preserve cache locality.

4) Backpressure and circuit-breakers
   - Circuit open threshold: error-rate > 10% or consecutive timeouts > 5 within 1 minute for an instance.
   - Throttle degradation: upon crossing 75% CPU or 80% queue depth, reduce per-tenant concurrency by 25% (configurable).

Concrete configuration table (recommended defaults)
-------------------------------------------------
| scope | key | default | notes |
|-------|-----|---------|-------|
| route | ingress.rate_limit.rps | 300 | interactive routes; override per-tier |
| route | ingress.burst_multiplier | 3.0 | max burst factor |
| route | ingress.max_queue | 200 | requests queued before 429 |
| runtime | fanout.max_replicas | 4 | documented in model manifest |
| runtime | fanout.fallback_variant_order | quantized,fp16,fp32 | router uses this order when reducing fanout |
| instance | circuit.error_rate_pct | 10 | rolling 60s window |
| instance | circuit.consecutive_timeouts | 5 | timeouts in 60s |
| scheduler | tenant.max_concurrency | 50 | soft limit; enforced by scheduler |

Examples (YAML configs)
-----------------------
api_route: 
  name: chat.v1.generate
  ingress: 
    rate_limit: 300
    burst_multiplier: 3.0
    max_queue: 200
  priority_class: interactive
  fanout: 
    max_replicas: 4
    fallback_candidates: ["redwood-7b-q4", "redwood-7b-fp16"]

Router pseudocode (behavioral example)
-------------------------------------
```
receive(request):
  if request.priority==best_effort and global_queue_depth > 10000:
    reject(429)
  route = select_route(request)
  if route.ingress.full():
    return 429 with x-retry-after
  replicas = pick_affine_replicas(route.fanout.max_replicas)
  for r in replicas:
    if r.circuit_open:
      continue
    send(r)
  if all attempts fail:
    fallback_to_variant(route.fanout.fallback_candidates[0])
```

Observability & SLOs
--------------------
- Exported metrics (per route, per model instance, per tenant):
  - request_rate (rps)
  - queue_depth
  - p50/p95/p99_latency_ms
  - error_rate_pct
  - fanout_inflight_replicas
  - circuit_state (open/half/closed)
- Dashboards: new service onboarding must include a traffic-shaping dashboard with: total ingress, queue depth, per-priority latencies, top rejected tenants, fanout distribution.
- Alerts (examples):
  - P95 latency for interactive routes > 120ms sustained for 5m -> P1 alert to oncall (Escalation playbook: increase capacity, enable emergency routing).
  - Queue depth > 80% of max_queue for 3m -> P2 alert to platform team.
  - Circuit open ratio > 10% of instances for 2m -> P2.

Rollout and testing guidance
---------------------------
1) Simulation tests before production change: feed synthetic traffic shaped to mix of priority classes. Validate p95/p99 latency and rejection rate under 1.5x expected peak.
2) Canary phases:
   - Step 1: Apply routing rule to 1% of traffic; run 30m with synthetic burst tests.
   - Step 2: 10% for 2 hours; monitor newly created dashboards.
   - Step 3: 100% after 24h with continuous monitoring.
3) Chaos scenario runbook:
   - Simulate a stuck instance by setting artificially high latency; ensure router respects circuit breaker and reduces fanout.
   - Validate fallback to quantized variant does not drop correctness beyond product-defined regression threshold (see quality-guardrails).

Security & Compliance considerations
----------------------------------
- Rate-limiting headers must be preserved and logged for auditing (x-tenant-id, x-route-id, x-rate-limit, x-retry-after).
- For Private deployments, local network QoS may override cloud ingress limits; document deviations in customer-specific runbooks.

Ownership and responsibilities
------------------------------
- Platform Networking & Router Team: implement ingress shaping primitives and fanout router (owner).
- Serving Runtime Team: expose circuit state and variant metadata via instance telemetry (collaborator).
- Observability Team: add dashboards and alert rules on onboarding checklist.
- Product: define per-plan defaults and priority class assignment.

Decision record (summary)
------------------------
We chose layered shaping + fanout reduction (instead of global reject-first approach) to: preserve low-latency service for premium users; minimize model-variant thrash; and enable predictable cost behavior. Alternatives considered: strict global queue (rejected for poor tenant isolation) and pure per-instance caps (insufficient for model-level cache locality).

Related pages and references
---------------------------
- Resource QoS and profiling playbook (infra-standards)
- ADR: request segmentation and priority routing (decision-records)
- Quality guardrails and fallback evaluation guidelines (applied-ml-and-evals)

Appendix: quick CLI test recipes
--------------------------------
- Simulate load: `ab -n 10000 -c 50 -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" https://api.redwood.ai/v1/chat`
- Check queue depth metric: `curl -s https://observability/api/metrics?name=queue_depth&route=chat.v1.generate`
- Force circuit open (dev only): `curl -X POST http://router-admin/instance/1234/simulate-latency -d '{"latency_ms": 10000}'`
